linkedin.text:
One business in a new FTC complaint paid about $47 a month for 4 years to lease a card machine. That's roughly $2,250 for a terminal that cost about $400 new.

The lease came bundled with a card processing deal from Riverside Payments, which the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and Washington state sued on Nov 2. The complaint says Riverside's quote sheets at times promised to cut up to 60% of a shop's card fees, and that shops that switched typically ended up paying more.

The rest of the fine print, as the FTC describes it: activation, batch, inactivity and data-security non-compliance fees left off the quote. A 26-page contract that ran 3 years and renewed on its own. $695 to leave. And a lease, through an affiliate, that ran a year past the contract, even though the pitch said shops could cancel at any time without penalty.

Riverside, its leasing affiliate and their two operators agreed to a proposed settlement. The order, which a judge still has to approve, has them pay $600,000 and gives customers 60 days to end the processing contract with no termination fee. According to OPB, it doesn't cover the machine leases.

Full disclosure: I started SVPay, which competes with processors like Riverside. So hold us to the same test as anyone. Before you sign, get four answers in writing: your all-in rate on a real statement (total fees ÷ card sales × 100), every fee by name, how long the contract runs and whether it renews on its own, and what it costs to leave, including any lease on the card machine.

Pull your last statement this week. How many separate fee lines are on it?

#SmallBusiness #Payments

facts.text: The FTC and Washington state sued Riverside Payments, its affiliate Cascade Equipment Leasing and operators Brandon Skinner and Jason Reese in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington (2:26-cv-04228); announced Nov 2, 2026
Riverside claimed businesses could save 40% to 60% by switching; businesses that switched typically paid more than with their prior provider (complaint para 43: 'over 40%, or nearly 60%')
Quote sheets omitted activation fees, batch fees, and fees for alleged data-security non-compliance or inactive processing
A roughly 26-page electronic contract; 3-year initial processing term with automatic renewal; $695 early termination fee (complaint paras 4, 47, 54, 56)
The equipment lease from Cascade auto-renews and runs one year longer than the processing contract

Complaint para 50: from 2020 to 2024 one small business in North Carolina paid approximately $47 per month for 4 years, a total of approximately $2,250, to lease a machine that would have cost around $400 to purchase new
Complaint para 47: the defendants represent that clients can cancel at any time without any penalty (press release: a 'no-risk' cancellation promise)
Settlement: Riverside, Cascade, Skinner and Reese pay $600,000; a $32,083,921 judgment is suspended after that payment
For 60 days Riverside waives the early termination fee and any penalty for rescinding processing agreements; the order takes effect when the district court judge approves and signs it

Case status: FTC and Washington v. Riverside Payments, matter 2523018, W.D. Wash.; complaint and stipulated proposed order filed Nov 2, 2026; FTC case page lists the case as Pending and does not show the order as entered (re-checked Nov 11, 2026)
OPB: the settlement does not cover the equipment leased by businesses; it goes to the chief magistrate judge in the Western District of Washington and could be approved any day

SVPay pricing: 'Simple pricing. Never per sale.' Processing and cash-out cost nothing on any plan; Starter is free, Growth and Pro are paid. Approved line used: SVPay makes money from paid software plans, never from a cut of your sales.
